content: I want to build an app to save and manage bookmarks.

Thanks — a bookmark app is a great place to start. Before I design anything, I want to make sure I understand what you're really after, so we build the right thing.

Let me start with the "why":

**When this app is finished and working well, what would be different or better in your day compared to how you handle bookmarks now?**

For example — are you frustrated that bookmarks are scattered across browsers and devices? That you save things and never find them again? That you can't organize or search them the way you want? Something else entirely?

Understanding the real pain behind "save and manage bookmarks" will shape everything, because "managing" can mean very different things depending on what's actually bothering you today.

The main problem is that I save useful links and then lose track of them. I want one calm, searchable place where I can quickly save a link, add a little context or a few labels, and find it again later—even if I only remember a word or topic.

I’d also like to separate things I still intend to read from things I’ve finished with, without having to delete useful links. Ideally, saving shouldn’t feel like data entry: the app should fill in the page details for me and let me adjust them when needed.

content:
That's really clear, and it tells me the heart of this is about *retrieval and peace of mind*, not just storage. Let me play back what I heard to make sure I've got the direction right:

**What I understood:**
- The core pain is **losing track** of useful links you've saved. So the whole point is being able to **find something again later**, even when you only half-remember it — just a word or a topic.
- You want saving to be **effortless** — the app pulls in the page's details for you, and you can tweak them if needed, rather than filling in a form.
- You want to add **a bit of your own context and a few labels** so it's findable on your terms.
- You want to tell apart **"still want to read"** from **"done with"** — but *keep* both, because a finished link is still useful. So it's less about deleting and more about a calm sense of what's pending vs. handled.
- Overall feeling: **calm**, not cluttered or effortful.

One thing I want to check on scope: it sounds like the *real* goal is **confidently finding a link again when you need it**, and the labels / read-vs-done separation are the *means* to keep the pile calm and searchable — rather than being the point in themselves. Does that framing feel right, or would you put the emphasis somewhere else?

And one practical question about where this lives: **what kind of app do you picture using — something in your web browser, on your phone, on your desktop, or a terminal-style tool?** This just helps me show you the right kind of working screen next.

Yes, that framing feels right. Finding things again is the main goal, and the labels and read status help keep everything manageable.

I picture it primarily as a web app I can use in a normal browser. I’d want it to work comfortably on both a computer and a phone, but it doesn’t need to be a separate mobile app.

- Paste a link and the app fills in the title, description, site icon, and a preview image for you; you can adjust anything, add a personal note, and add labels (with your past labels suggested for reuse).
- New saves are marked "Read later" by default; you can turn that off.

**Finding** (your main goal)
- A search that looks across titles, descriptions, your notes, labels, and addresses, matching a half-remembered word anywhere, case-insensitively, with matches highlighted.
- Precise refinements: `#label`, `"exact phrases"`, and `AND`/`OR`/`NOT` with parentheses; quote a word to search it literally.

**Keeping it calm**
- Open a link's page by clicking its title or icon (opens in a new tab, list stays put).
- Mark links "read" or move them back — never deleting them — and focus with **All / To read / Finished** views that carry counts and combine with search.
- Sort by newest, oldest, or title, with your choice remembered.
- Welcoming empty state, tidy long titles, and a design that keeps the important details prominent.

I've also noted two things for the build itself: keeping the list calm-looking (visual prominence) and staying fast with hundreds of links.

That completes **all eight additional areas** — everything you asked to settle is now agreed. Here's the full picture that's locked in (22 usage flows):

**Saving & capturing**
- Effortless save with auto-filled title, description, icon, and preview; adjust anything, add a note and labels; "Read later" by default.
- Unreadable pages still save (you title them); non-link text is refused; re-pasting opens the existing one (no duplicates), editable including the address with a clash safeguard.

Fixed and re-verified. The empty-state bug is resolved.

## What was wrong and the fix
It was an **implementation error** against the empty-state behaviour we approved (SCN-010): a CSS rule made the dark **bulk-action bar** show even when hidden, and the empty **filter pill** and controls row weren't hidden with nothing saved — so first use looked broken.

**Corrected:**
- Hidden elements now always truly hide (a global CSS rule), so the bulk bar never shows unless links are selected.
- With **no bookmarks**, the whole controls row (filter, sort, Archived), the saved-searches row, and the bulk bar are hidden entirely — leaving just the title, the save bar, the search box, and the welcoming message.

Here's the corrected first-use screen (also saved for you at `prototypes/empty-state-fixed.png`):

- Clean empty state — no dark bar, no blank pill.

- **20 unit tests** — unchanged, still green.
- **13 acceptance tests** — including a **strengthened SCN-010 test** that now asserts the controls row, bulk bar, saved-searches row, and filter are all hidden on first use (locking this so it can't regress). All pass.
